What Tichenor can't tell us: whether courts will ultimately impose meaningful restraint, or continue patterns of deference that have historically let presidential overreach go unchecked in immigration. The doctrinal tools exist. Whether they get used is a different question.

The INA is implicated too. Tichenor examines efforts to detain and remove people for pro-Palestinian speech using national security authority in the INA against First Amendment-protected activity. Courts have not resolved how far this extends.

Tichenor's argument: the current administration isn't just using broad presidential power over immigration, it's claiming emergency prerogative powers normally reserved for declared wars to run a mass deportation program.

The plenary power doctrine gave the political branches near-unchecked control over who enters and who gets removed. That deference, built for sovereign border control, is now being stretched to cover peacetime mass deportation via wartime law.

Tichenor traces presidential dominance over immigration to four forces: elastic Article II language, the plenary power doctrine (1880s onward), congressional gridlock fueling unilateral action, and emergency powers originally designed for wartime.

The Alien Enemies Act has been invoked three times in US history: War of 1812, WWI, WWII. All three followed a formal declaration of war by Congress. The current invocation meets none of those historical benchmarks.

The full Cerón & Patler study is open access in the Journal on Migration and Human Security. 

LINK: doi.org/10.1177/233150242614…

I've been writing about what detention does to people. This study extends that picture across the border.
LINK: austinkocher.substack.com/p/…

What this study can't tell us: whether these harms persist weeks or months after return, or how they compound with pre-existing trauma from the migration journey. Cross-sectional data at the moment of deportation is the study's strength and its limit.

ICE's detained population hit 70,500+ by late January 2026, the highest in the system's modern history. The Laken Riley Act now mandates detention for people accused, not convicted, of low-level offenses.

Worth noting: the average detention length in this sample was under 2 months. These aren't people who spent years inside. The health signal is detectable even at relatively short exposure, which matters a lot as the system detains more people faster.

The largest effect: deported migrants who rated their treatment by immi authorities as poor had 2.91x the odds of reporting poor health versus those who reported good treatment. That's not a marginal association and it persisted across every sensitivity analysis the authors ran.

The study tested 3 dimensions: physical abuse, verbal abuse, and perceived poor treatment by immi authorities. All 3 were independently associated with worse health after deportation even after controlling for age, detention length, country of origin, and arresting agency.

Deported Central Americans who experienced physical abuse in US immigration custody had nearly 70% higher odds of reporting poor health immediately after deportation. This is what detention does and it doesn't stop at the border.

“Acting Director.” a reminder that there has been no congressionally confirmed Director of Immigration and customs enforcement since January 19, 2017 — 3400 days.


Priscilla Alvarez (@priscialva)

BREAKING: David Venturella is expected to serve as the next acting ICE director, according to a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson. cnn.com/2026/05/12/politics/…

What "voluntary departure" means legally: no formal removal order, which theoretically makes future legal return easier. But Vera's researchers are clear that for people departing from detention under these conditions, calling it voluntary misrepresents the coercion involved.

Geography shows up here too. Texas (12,400) and Louisiana (5,400) led voluntary departure orders in the Sep. 2025–Feb. 2026 period. Both states have high concentrations of detained immigrants and historically restrictive immigration courts.

What "voluntary departure" means legally: no formal removal order, which theoretically makes future legal return easier. But Vera's researchers are clear that for people departing from detention under these conditions, calling it voluntary misrepresents the coercion involved.

Geography shows up here too. Texas (12,400) and Louisiana (5,400) led voluntary departure orders in the Sep. 2025–Feb. 2026 period. Both states have high concentrations of detained immigrants and historically restrictive immigration courts.

Vera's researchers also found that newly appointed, inexperienced immigration judges, hired under threat of dismissal, are disproportionately assigned to detained dockets and are granting voluntary departure at higher rates than veteran judges.

The spike tracks specific policy changes: the July 2025 ICE memo declaring detained immigrants ineligible for bond hearings. Once you remove the possibility of release pending your case, the calculus for detained people shifts dramatically.
